pieces.title: Street architecture
pieces.brief:
Build the block the game is played on: a 1925 Manhattan side street canyon that reads instantly as New York and never as generic old city.

What has to exist and be modelled with real proportions from docs/PERIOD-REFERENCE.md: five- and six-storey tenements on 25ft lots with the correct floor heights; red brick and brownstone facades that differ building to building; window openings with lintels, sills and sashes (some open, some with a face or a cat or a flowerpot in them); cornices with real overhang and shadow; fire escapes as actual iron geometry — stringers, treads, landings, drop ladders — because the ball is going to hit them; stoops with the right step count and width, with railings and areaways below; basement shop entries; awnings; roof water towers on their timber frames; chimney pots; parapets; painted ghost signs on the exposed side wall of a corner building; and at the far end of the street, the elevated railway on its lattice columns crossing the view.

Storefronts at street level with period business types and hand-lettered signage drawn from the reference (grocer, barber, tailor, cigar store, delicatessen, shoe repair, five-and-dime). Letter them legibly — signage is where the period lives. Generate lettering procedurally onto canvas textures; embed nothing from the network.

Composition matters more than square footage: the camera looks down the street, so build depth cues — receding cornice lines, a break in the wall for an alley, a corner building that closes the far end, sunlight on one facade and shade on the other. The playing surface must stay readable: nothing between the camera and the plate, nothing that makes the ball hard to see.

Instance repeated geometry (windows, bricks, fire-escape treads) — you own the biggest polygon budget in the game and must stay inside a 60fps frame at 1600x900.

Register scenarios 'block_tour' (a slow camera showing the whole block) and 'facade_detail' (close on one tenement front so a critic can judge the craft).

pieces.title: Surface and props
pieces.brief:
Everything on the ground, and everything that makes the street look lived in.

The playing surface: Belgian block and patched asphalt with the wear pattern of a real street — a worn centre, oil stains, tar seams, puddles after rain, trolley tracks if the reference supports them on this kind of block, and painted-out old markings. The manhole cover is home plate and must be a proper cast-iron cover with real lettering; chalk bases scrawled on the asphalt; a chalked strike box on the wall behind the batter; hopscotch and other kids' chalk left over near the sidewalk. Curbs, gutters, sewer grates the ball can vanish into, coal chutes, cellar doors.

The props: fire hydrant (period design), bishop's-crook lamp posts, fire alarm box, mailbox, ash cans and trash, wooden crates, a newsstand with period papers, a pushcart with produce, milk bottles on a stoop, a bicycle, a stickball bat leaning on a railing, broom handles, a Spaldeen or two, laundry lines strung between buildings with real cloth, window boxes, a barber pole, a dog.

Vehicles: a parked Model T or two with correct silhouette and period colours, a delivery truck with hand-painted signage on its panel, a horse cart or ice wagon. These are gameplay objects as much as scenery — the ball caroms off them, so place them where a carom is fun, not where it blocks the view.

Dress with intent, not clutter: every prop should either tell you about the neighbourhood, give the ball something to do, or frame the composition. Everything must be procedural geometry plus canvas textures; instance anything repeated.

Register 'surface_detail' (camera low over the plate showing pavement, chalk and manhole) and 'props_tour'.

pieces.title: Sky, light and air
pieces.brief:
Make the air in the street do the emotional work.

Sky: a real gradient sky for a late-September New York afternoon, with the sun low enough that a five-storey wall throws a hard diagonal across the pavement. Clouds with period character (not photoreal HDR), a hazy horizon, and the specific quality of light in a narrow canyon: direct warm sun on the upper storeys and one side of the street, cool bounced skylight in the shade, warm reflected light coming back off the sunlit brick.

Lighting: build the key/fill/bounce rig so kids read as three-dimensional and the ball stays the brightest object in the frame at all times — that is a hard requirement, the ball must never be lost against pavement or brick. Contact shadows under every character and prop. Shadow quality that holds up at 1600x900 without shimmering.

Air: coal-smoke haze with distance, chimney smoke drifting, dust motes in the sun shafts, heat shimmer off tar. Pigeons that flock, land on cornices, and scatter when the ball comes near. Laundry that moves in the wind. A wind direction all systems can read from a shared value.

A time-of-day control that at minimum supports the default late-afternoon look and a golden-hour late-innings look, so the game can change mood as it goes on. Keep both readable and cheerful — sooty must never become grim.

Register 'golden_hour' and 'atmosphere' (a shot composed to show smoke, pigeons, laundry and light shafts together).

pieces.title: Art direction and shading
pieces.brief:
You own the look. Every other system imports its colours from src/render/palette.js and its materials from src/render/materials.js, so your job is to make one coherent visual language and publish it as an API the other pieces use.

Decide and implement the shading model the design bible calls for: a toon/painterly treatment that keeps Backyard Baseball's warmth and readability while the subject matter is sooty 1925 brick. That likely means banded lighting ramps with warm-to-cool shadow shifts rather than grey shadows, a controlled outline treatment on characters and gameplay-critical objects (not on everything — outlining the whole city will look like a coloring book), and hand-made surface texture rather than photoreal roughness maps.

Publish from palette.js: named colour tokens for pavement, brick families, brownstone, sky, skin tones, the two team kits, the ball, chalk, iron, wood, and the accent reserved for readability. Publish helpers so other systems never invent a hex value.

Publish from materials.js: a small set of shared, cached materials (toon-lit, unlit, outlined, chalk, iron, glass) with the outline pass wired in, so draw calls stay low.

Build the post pass in postfx.js: colour grade toward the bible's look, a subtle vignette, and whatever film-like grain or bloom the bible allows — restrained, and it must never hurt the readability of the ball. Everything must degrade gracefully if the device can't afford it.

Make a 'style_sheet' scenario: a composed frame showing the palette applied to real geometry — a brick wall, a stoop, a kid, a ball, chalk, iron, sky — that a critic can judge the whole art direction from in one image.
